title: Animal Movements Game
strapline: Jump like a frog, waddle like a penguin, crawl like a bear — listening with your whole body.
intent: Children develop gross motor skills through a wide range of contrasting movements.
Listening for the animal name and responding is real, active listening practice.
Children learn animal characteristics by embodying them rather than being told.
Imagining themselves as an animal builds imagination and confidence in front of others.
A game with no losers lets every child take part at their own level.
implementation: Clear a decent space, indoors or out, with room to move safely.
Call out different animals and let children move like them — jump like a frog, waddle like a penguin, crawl like a bear.
Join in fully yourself; children move more freely when the adult looks silly too.
Introduce descriptive movement words as you go: hop, slither, stretch, swing, stomp.
Let children choose the next animal so the game belongs to them.
Vary the pace deliberately — a fast cheetah then a slow tortoise builds control.
Add a freeze or a "sleeping animals" rest so the game has quiet in it too.
key_questions: How does that animal move? Can you show me?
Which animal moves the fastest? The slowest?
Can you move like that but very quietly?
What animal shall we be next — you choose.
How does your body feel after all that jumping?

impact.text: Children run, hop, crawl and balance with confidence and control.
Children listen and respond in a group and shift attention when the call changes.
Children follow two-part instructions in a fast-moving game.
Children take up descriptive movement vocabulary and use it themselves.
Children contribute ideas to the group and grow in confidence doing it.
Children notice what their body needs — hot, tired, thirsty — and act on it.

enhancements: Animal masks from the Art/Design activity worn during the game.
A music version where the tempo tells you which animal to be.
An obstacle course crossed as different animals.
Photograph cards of real animals moving, used as the prompts.
A child-led version where one child is the caller for the whole group.
An outdoor habitat trail — move like the animal that lives in each zone.

playing_exploring: Children invent their own version of each animal's movement.
The game is pure open-ended physical play with nothing to get wrong.
active_learning: Children keep going through a physically demanding game.
They push themselves to hold a hard position or move faster.
creating_thinking: Children work out how an animal must move from what they know about it.
They compare and contrast animals through their bodies.
